result:
The Voyager probes, launched in 1977, remain two of humanity’s most remarkable artifacts. Voyager 1 is now more than 15 billion miles from Earth, traveling through interstellar space at roughly 38,000 miles per hour; Voyager 2 follows a different trajectory but has also crossed the heliopause. Both still send back faint data, their plutonium power sources slowly fading. Attached to each is a gold-plated copper phonograph record—the Golden Record—intended as a greeting to any civilization that might one day intercept the spacecraft.

The record contains 115 analog images, a variety of natural sounds (surf, wind, thunder, birds, whales), spoken greetings in 55 languages, and 90 minutes of music ranging from Bach and Beethoven to Indonesian gamelan, Navajo chants, and Chuck Berry’s “Johnny B. Goode.” Carl Sagan and his team chose the contents with deliberate care, aiming for a representative sample of Earth’s diversity rather than a boastful catalog of achievements. Instructions for playing the record are etched in pictorial form, along with a pulsar map that locates our solar system in the galaxy.

Whether any extraterrestrial intelligence will ever find and decode it is vanishingly unlikely. The probes will wander the Milky Way for billions of years, their trajectories perturbed by distant stars long after the Sun has become a white dwarf. The Golden Record is therefore less a practical message than a time capsule of late-20th-century human self-conception: curious, hopeful, and aware of its own smallness. In that sense it already succeeded. It forced a group of scientists and artists to decide, under deadline, what was worth saying about ourselves to the cosmos. The result is both touching and incomplete, which may be the most honest portrait possible.
